subject: General Surgery
stem: A trauma patient opens his eyes to painful stimulus, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from pain. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is
explanation: Eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds score 2 and withdrawal from pain scores 4, totalling 8. A score of 8 or less defines severe head injury and is the conventional threshold for intubation.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The lowest possible Glasgow Coma Scale score is
explanation: Each of the three components has a minimum of 1, so the scale runs from 3 to 15. In intubated patients the verbal score cannot be assessed and is recorded with a modifier rather than scored as 1 silently.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In the primary survey of a trauma patient, the correct order of priorities is
explanation: ATLS teaches that the greatest threat is treated first. Catastrophic external haemorrhage is the one recognised exception, handled before or alongside the airway in the C-ABC modification used in military practice.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Class III haemorrhagic shock in an adult corresponds to a blood loss of
explanation: Class III is the first class with frank hypotension and reduced urine output, and it mandates blood rather than crystalloid alone. Class II shows tachycardia with a narrowed pulse pressure but a preserved systolic pressure.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The earliest reliable clinical sign of compensated haemorrhagic shock in a young adult is
options: A fall in systolic blood pressure
A narrowed pulse pressure with tachycardia
explanation: Diastolic pressure rises with catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction before systolic pressure falls, so pulse pressure narrows first. A young patient can lose 30% of blood volume before the systolic pressure drops.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In damage control resuscitation for massive haemorrhage, blood products are given in a ratio of
options: 1:1:1 packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets
explanation: The PROPPR trial supported balanced transfusion. Permissive hypotension, limited crystalloid, warming, calcium replacement and early tranexamic acid within 3 hours complete the strategy against the lethal triad.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The lethal triad of trauma consists of
explanation: Each worsens the others, which is why damage control surgery aims at rapid control rather than definitive repair, with the patient returned to theatre after physiological correction. Hyperglycaemia is sometimes added as a fourth element.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A trauma patient has distended neck veins, hypotension and muffled heart sounds after a steering-wheel injury. The immediate step is
explanation: This is traumatic tamponade. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma shows pericardial fluid in seconds; definitive treatment is surgical, as the bleeding source needs repair.
exam: 2024 INI-CET medicine (Beck triad in tamponade), 2022 INI-CET (chest trauma)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET medicine (Beck triad in tamponade), 2022 INI-CET (chest trauma)

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest site of aortic injury in blunt deceleration trauma is
options: Just distal to the left subclavian artery at the ligamentum arteriosum
explanation: The descending aorta is tethered there while the arch moves freely. A widened mediastinum on the chest film prompts CT angiography; repair is usually endovascular now.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An indication for emergency thoracotomy after chest tube insertion for haemothorax is
options: An initial drainage of more than 1,500 mL, or more than 200 mL per hour for 3 hours
explanation: This marks ongoing bleeding from a systemic vessel, usually intercostal or internal mammary, which will not stop with drainage alone. A persistent air leak needs bronchoscopy to exclude tracheobronchial injury.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (chest trauma and drainage), 2024 INI-CET (thoracic injury)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (chest trauma and drainage), 2024 INI-CET (thoracic injury)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Flail chest is defined as
options: Fracture of a single rib in two places
Fracture of two or more contiguous ribs in two or more places, producing paradoxical movement
explanation: The underlying pulmonary contusion, not the chest wall motion, causes hypoxia. Management is analgesia, physiotherapy and ventilatory support, with surgical fixation in selected patients.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which structure is most commonly injured in blunt abdominal trauma requiring laparotomy in adults?
explanation: The liver is the next most commonly injured. Left lower rib fractures should raise suspicion of splenic injury; non-operative management with angioembolisation is now standard in the haemodynamically stable patient.

subject: General Surgery
stem: FAST examination in trauma assesses all of the following spaces EXCEPT
explanation: Ultrasound cannot reliably see the retroperitoneum, so it misses pancreatic, duodenal and renal injuries; CT is needed for those. Extended FAST adds the thoracic windows for pneumothorax and haemothorax.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (blunt abdominal trauma assessment), 2024 INI-CET (imaging in trauma)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (blunt abdominal trauma assessment), 2024 INI-CET (imaging in trauma)

subject: General Surgery
stem: A haemodynamically stable patient with blunt abdominal trauma and free fluid on FAST should next have
explanation: CT grades solid organ injury and detects contrast blush, allowing non-operative management. Instability with positive FAST mandates laparotomy without CT; lavage is now largely obsolete.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Blood at the external urethral meatus with a high-riding prostate after pelvic fracture means
explanation: Blind catheterisation can convert a partial posterior urethral tear into a complete one. A suprapubic catheter diverts urine, and repair is delayed for about 3 months.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest site of urethral injury in a fall astride (straddle) injury is the
explanation: The bulb is crushed against the inferior border of the pubis. Pelvic fractures instead shear the membranous urethra at the urogenital diaphragm. Butterfly perineal bruising follows a bulbar injury.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In extradural haematoma, the artery most often torn and the classic clinical course are
options: Middle meningeal artery; progressive drowsiness without lucidity
Middle meningeal artery; a lucid interval after brief loss of consciousness
Bridging veins; fluctuating consciousness in the elderly
explanation: A biconvex hyperdense collection limited by sutures appears on CT, usually with a temporal bone fracture. Option C describes a chronic subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A crescentic hyperdense collection crossing suture lines in an elderly man on warfarin after minor trauma is
explanation: Subdural blood spreads along the whole convexity because the subdural space is not limited by sutures, whereas extradural blood is. Brain atrophy stretches the bridging veins, making the elderly vulnerable.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (head injury types), 2024 INI-CET (CT in head trauma)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (head injury types), 2024 INI-CET (CT in head trauma)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Cushing reflex in raised intracranial pressure consists of
explanation: It is a late, ominous sign of impending herniation. Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, and is kept above 60 mmHg with head elevation, osmotherapy and normocapnia.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (head injury management), 2024 INI-CET medicine (Beck triad contrast)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (head injury management), 2024 INI-CET medicine (Beck triad contrast)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Cerebral perfusion pressure is calculated as
options: Mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure
Mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure
Diastolic pressure plus one-third of pulse pressure
explanation: Option D is the formula for mean arterial pressure itself. Hyperventilation lowers intracranial pressure through vasoconstriction but is reserved for brief use, since it risks ischaemia.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In the Wallace rule of nines for an adult, the burnt surface area of one entire lower limb is
explanation: Head and each upper limb are 9% each, the front and back of the trunk 18% each, each lower limb 18%, and the perineum 1%. Children have proportionally larger heads, so the Lund and Browder chart is used.
exam: 2022 INI-CET / 2021 INI-CET (rule of nines and burn area, 3X)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET / 2021 INI-CET (rule of nines and burn area, 3X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 70 kg adult with 40% burns receives, by the Parkland formula, a first-24-hour crystalloid volume of
explanation: Four mL multiplied by 70 kg by 40% gives 11,200 mL of Ringer lactate, half in the first 8 hours from the time of injury and half over the next 16. Urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hour guides titration.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A burn wound that is dry, leathery, insensate and does not blanch is
explanation: Destroyed nerve endings make it painless, and it needs excision with grafting. Superficial partial-thickness burns are moist, painful and blanch on pressure, and heal in 2 to 3 weeks without grafting.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The topical agent of choice for a burn involving cartilage, as on the ear, is
explanation: It penetrates eschar and cartilage, but causes pain and a carbonic anhydrase inhibition that produces metabolic acidosis. Silver sulfadiazine causes transient leucopenia and does not penetrate eschar well.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Inhalational injury in a burns patient is suggested by all of the following EXCEPT
options: Singed nasal hairs and carbonaceous sputum
A history of burns in a closed space
explanation: Pulse oximetry is unreliable because carboxyhaemoglobin reads as oxyhaemoglobin. Early intubation is undertaken before oedema makes the airway impassable; bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis.
exam: 2021 INI-CET (burn assessment), 2022 INI-CET medicine (pulse oximetry limitations)

metadata.basedOn: 2021 INI-CET (burn assessment), 2022 INI-CET medicine (pulse oximetry limitations)

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of death in the first 24 hours after a major burn is
options: Hypovolaemic shock, and airway compromise from inhalational injury
explanation: Sepsis, usually from *Pseudomonas* or *Staphylococcus*, dominates later mortality. Early excision with grafting and enteral feeding reduce it; prophylactic systemic antibiotics do not help.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Circumferential full-thickness burns of a limb with absent distal pulses require
explanation: The inelastic eschar, not raised compartment pressure, is the constricting element, so incising it suffices. A circumferential chest burn restricting ventilation also needs escharotomy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest organism causing invasive burn wound infection is
explanation: It produces a blue-green exudate with a characteristic odour. *Staphylococcus aureus* dominates the earliest colonisation. Quantitative wound biopsy, not swab culture, distinguishes colonisation from invasion.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 45-year-old woman has a 3 cm mobile breast lump with two mobile ipsilateral axillary nodes and no distant disease. The clinical stage is
explanation: T2 with N1 is stage IIB. T2N0 would be IIA, and T3N1 or any N2 disease would be IIIA. T2 spans tumours above 2 cm and up to 5 cm.
exam: 2024 INI-CET / 2022 INI-CET (TNM staging of breast carcinoma, 3X)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET / 2022 INI-CET (TNM staging of breast carcinoma, 3X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which breast tumour size defines T3 in the TNM system?
explanation: T1 is up to 2 cm, T2 is 2 to 5 cm, T3 is above 5 cm, and T4 is any size with chest wall or skin involvement including peau d'orange, satellite nodules or inflammatory carcinoma.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Peau d'orange appearance of the breast skin is caused by
options: Retraction of the ligaments of Cooper
explanation: Skin tethered at hair follicles cannot swell, producing the pitted appearance. Option C causes skin dimpling and nipple retraction instead. Peau d'orange makes the tumour T4b.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Sentinel lymph node biopsy in breast cancer is contraindicated in
options: A T1 tumour with a clinically normal axilla
Ductal carcinoma in situ undergoing mastectomy
A multifocal tumour with a normal axilla
explanation: Palpable disease requires axillary dissection, since the sentinel node concept assumes an undisturbed, uninvolved basin. Dual mapping with blue dye and radiocolloid gives the highest identification rate.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The level of axillary nodes defined by their relation to the pectoralis minor as lying deep to the muscle is
explanation: Level I lies lateral and below the muscle, level II behind it, and level III medial to it at the apex. Rotter nodes lie between the pectoralis major and minor. A level I and II clearance is the standard dissection.

subject: General Surgery
stem: During axillary dissection, injury to which nerve causes a winged scapula?
explanation: It supplies serratus anterior. Thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi and shoulder extension, and intercostobrachial division causes numbness over the inner upper arm, the commonest sensory complaint after surgery.
exam: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (nerve injury in axillary surgery, 2X)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (nerve injury in axillary surgery, 2X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Triple-negative breast cancer means the tumour lacks
options: All three hormone receptors with high HER2
Progesterone receptor, HER2 and BRCA mutation
Oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 expression
explanation: It is commoner in young women and in *BRCA1* carriers, and is not helped by endocrine or anti-HER2 therapy, so chemotherapy with platinum and immunotherapy or PARP inhibition is used.
exam: 2024 INI-CET (breast cancer receptor status and therapy, 2X)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET (breast cancer receptor status and therapy, 2X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Trastuzumab therapy requires monitoring of
explanation: Its cardiotoxicity is usually reversible, unlike the dose-dependent irreversible injury from anthracyclines, so the two are preferably not given together. HER2 positivity on immunohistochemistry or FISH is required before use.
exam: 2024 INI-CET (HER2 and targeted therapy), 2022 INI-CET pharmacology (anticancer toxicity)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET (HER2 and targeted therapy), 2022 INI-CET pharmacology (anticancer toxicity)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Tamoxifen increases the risk of
explanation: It is an antagonist in the breast but an agonist in the endometrium and bone, so it protects bone. Aromatase inhibitors, used after menopause, cause osteoporosis and arthralgia instead.
exam: 2024 INI-CET (hormone receptor status and endocrine therapy), 2022 INI-CET pharmacology (SERMs)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET (hormone receptor status and endocrine therapy), 2022 INI-CET pharmacology (SERMs)

subject: General Surgery
stem: An aromatase inhibitor such as letrozole is appropriate for
options: A premenopausal woman without ovarian suppression
A postmenopausal woman with hormone receptor-positive disease
explanation: Before menopause, the ovary makes oestrogen independently of aromatase, so an inhibitor alone fails and may paradoxically stimulate the ovary unless a GnRH agonist is added.
exam: 2024 INI-CET (endocrine therapy choice), 2022 INI-CET (breast cancer management)

metadata.basedOn: 2024 INI-CET (endocrine therapy choice), 2022 INI-CET (breast cancer management)

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 22-year-old has a firm, smooth, highly mobile 2 cm breast lump. The diagnosis and management are
options: Fibroadenoma; triple assessment with reassurance or excision if symptomatic
explanation: The "breast mouse" is a hyperplastic lobule, not a true neoplasm, and many involute after menopause. Rapid growth in a larger lump raises suspicion of a phyllodes tumour, which needs wide local excision.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which feature distinguishes a phyllodes tumour from a fibroadenoma?
options: Rapid growth with stromal hypercellularity and leaf-like architecture
explanation: Treatment is wide local excision with a 1 cm margin, because enucleation leads to recurrence. Spread, when it occurs, is haematogenous to the lung, so axillary dissection is unnecessary.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (benign and borderline breast tumours), 2024 INI-CET (breast pathology)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (benign and borderline breast tumours), 2024 INI-CET (breast pathology)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Blood-stained nipple discharge from a single duct in a 40-year-old is most often due to
explanation: Carcinoma must still be excluded by imaging and ductoscopy or microdochectomy. Duct ectasia gives a green or creamy multi-duct discharge with a slit-like nipple retraction, often in smokers.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Paget disease of the nipple is characterised by
options: An eczematous areola that spares the nipple
An eczematous nipple with underlying in-situ or invasive carcinoma
Bilateral nipple itching responding to steroids
explanation: It starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola, whereas eczema does the reverse and spares the nipple. Full-thickness nipple biopsy shows large pale Paget cells; imaging of the whole breast follows.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A lactating woman has a tender, fluctuant, erythematous breast swelling with fever. The management is
options: Immediate wide incision and drainage with weaning
Ultrasound-guided aspiration with antibiotics, continuing breastfeeding
explanation: *Staphylococcus aureus* is the usual organism. Feeding or expression from the affected side should continue to prevent stasis. Formal drainage is needed only for a large or multiloculated collection.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Non-lactational periductal mastitis with a mammillary fistula is most strongly associated with
explanation: Anaerobic organisms predominate, so metronidazole with a beta-lactam is used. Recurrent fistula needs excision of the affected duct system, and continued smoking makes recurrence likely.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Fat necrosis of the breast after trauma is important chiefly because
options: It mimics carcinoma clinically and on mammography
explanation: A hard, irregular mass with skin tethering and calcification is produced, so triple assessment with core biopsy is needed. Once confirmed, it needs no treatment and resolves slowly.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (benign breast disease), 2024 INI-CET (breast lump evaluation)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (benign breast disease), 2024 INI-CET (breast lump evaluation)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Gynaecomastia in an adolescent male is most commonly
explanation: Pubertal gynaecomastia resolves within about 2 years in most boys. Drugs — spironolactone, digoxin, cimetidine, ketoconazole, anabolic steroids — and cirrhosis, hyperthyroidism and testicular tumours must be excluded when it persists.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (breast disorders in men), 2024 INI-CET (hormonal effects)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (breast disorders in men), 2024 INI-CET (hormonal effects)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy is contraindicated in
options: A 2 cm tumour in a large breast
Multicentric disease, prior chest radiotherapy, or pregnancy in the first trimester
explanation: Survival after conservation equals that after mastectomy when clear margins and radiotherapy are achieved, so tumour biology and nodal status do not by themselves rule it out.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest site of distant metastasis in breast carcinoma is
explanation: Spread is through Batson's vertebral venous plexus, giving osteolytic deposits in the vertebrae, pelvis and femur. Lung, liver and brain follow. Bone scan or PET-CT is used for staging in symptomatic or advanced disease.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Charcot triad of acute cholangitis consists of
options: Fever with chills, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain
explanation: Adding hypotension and altered mental state gives the Reynolds pentad of suppurative cholangitis, which needs urgent biliary decompression by ERCP alongside antibiotics and resuscitation.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Courvoisier law states that a palpable, non-tender gall bladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to
options: Stones in the common bile duct
explanation: Chronic cholecystitis accompanying stones leaves the gall bladder fibrotic and unable to distend. Recognised exceptions include a double impacted stone and oriental cholangiohepatitis.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The investigation of choice for suspected choledocholithiasis in a patient with a dilated duct and deranged liver enzymes is
options: CT of the abdomen without contrast
explanation: It is non-invasive and highly sensitive for ductal stones. ERCP is then therapeutic rather than diagnostic, and endoscopic ultrasound is an alternative when MRCP is equivocal.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Calot triangle is bounded by
options: The common bile duct, the portal vein and the duodenum
The cystic duct, the cystic artery and the liver
The cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver
The cystic duct, the right hepatic artery and the gall bladder fundus
explanation: The cystic artery usually runs within it, which is why the critical view of safety requires both tubular structures to be identified before any clipping during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Mirizzi syndrome refers to
options: Gall bladder carcinoma invading the liver
A gallstone eroding into the duodenum
Obstruction of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch
explanation: Extrinsic compression or a cholecystocholedochal fistula results. It raises the risk of bile duct injury greatly, so subtotal cholecystectomy is often safer than attempting a complete dissection.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Pneumobilia with small bowel obstruction and an ectopic gallstone on imaging indicates
options: Gallstone ileus through a cholecystoduodenal fistula
explanation: That is Rigler triad. The stone lodges most often at the terminal ileum, the narrowest point. Enterolithotomy relieves the obstruction, with fistula repair deferred or omitted in frail patients.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (gall bladder disease complications), 2024 INI-CET (small bowel obstruction)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (gall bladder disease complications), 2024 INI-CET (small bowel obstruction)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Prophylactic cholecystectomy is indicated for an asymptomatic gall bladder in
options: Porcelain gall bladder, stones above 3 cm, or an associated polyp above 1 cm
explanation: Each carries a raised risk of gall bladder carcinoma. Small stones instead predispose to pancreatitis through migration. Routine cholecystectomy for silent stones is not justified.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (gall bladder stones and malignancy), 2024 INI-CET (gall bladder carcinoma)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (gall bladder stones and malignancy), 2024 INI-CET (gall bladder carcinoma)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Gall bladder carcinoma most often arises in
options: The fundus, and spreads early to segments IV and V of the liver
explanation: Its thin wall lacks a muscularis mucosae, which allows early invasion. A T1a tumour found incidentally after cholecystectomy needs no further surgery, while T1b and above need extended resection.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A Klatskin tumour is a cholangiocarcinoma at
options: The hilar confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts
explanation: The Bismuth–Corlette classification grades its ductal extent. Primary sclerosing cholangitis, choledochal cyst, liver fluke infestation and hepatolithiasis are the recognised risk factors.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which type of choledochal cyst is commonest, and what is its treatment?
options: Type I fusiform dilatation of the common bile duct; excision with hepaticojejunostomy
explanation: Drainage alone is inadequate, because the retained epithelium carries a high risk of cholangiocarcinoma. An anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction permitting pancreatic reflux is the usual aetiology.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 6-week-old infant has persistent conjugated jaundice, pale stools and a firm liver. The operation and the window for best outcome are
options: Kasai portoenterostomy, ideally before 8 weeks of age
explanation: Biliary atresia causes progressive fibrosis, so delay reduces the chance of establishing bile flow. A triangular-cord sign on ultrasound and absent gall bladder support the diagnosis; many still need transplantation later.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide is
explanation: Alcohol is next. A lipase or amylase above three times the upper limit with typical pain establishes the diagnosis, and contrast CT is deferred for 72 to 96 hours to assess necrosis accurately.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Grey Turner sign in severe acute pancreatitis refers to
options: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the legs
explanation: Cullen sign is the periumbilical equivalent, and Fox sign is bruising over the inguinal ligament. All are late and uncommon, and none is needed for diagnosis.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The cornerstone of early management of severe acute pancreatitis is
options: Goal-directed fluid resuscitation with early enteral nutrition and analgesia
explanation: Enteral feeding preserves gut barrier function and lowers infective complications. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended, and intervention for necrosis is delayed about 4 weeks and done by a step-up approach.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (acute pancreatitis management), 2024 INI-CET (critical care nutrition)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (acute pancreatitis management), 2024 INI-CET (critical care nutrition)

subject: General Surgery
stem: A fluid collection in the lesser sac persisting 6 weeks after acute pancreatitis, with a well-defined wall, is
options: An abscess requiring immediate open drainage
A pseudocyst, drained only if symptomatic or above about 6 cm
Walled-off necrosis requiring necrosectomy in all cases
explanation: It lacks an epithelial lining, which is why it is called a pseudocyst. Endoscopic cystogastrostomy is now preferred to open drainage when the cyst abuts the stomach wall.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The Whipple procedure for carcinoma of the pancreatic head removes
options: The pancreatic body and tail with the spleen
The whole pancreas with the spleen
The pancreatic head, duodenum, gall bladder, distal bile duct and, classically, the distal stomach
explanation: The pylorus-preserving modification retains the antrum. Only about 20% of tumours are resectable at presentation, and involvement of the superior mesenteric artery or coeliac axis makes them unresectable.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The tumour marker most used to follow pancreatic adenocarcinoma is
explanation: It is unreliable in obstructive jaundice, since cholestasis raises it independently, and is falsely normal in Lewis antigen-negative individuals. It is used for monitoring rather than screening.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Chronic calcific pancreatitis with a dilated main duct above 7 mm and intractable pain is best treated by
explanation: A dilated duct suits drainage, whereas head-dominant inflammatory disease suits a Frey or Beger resection. Tropical calcific pancreatitis is the common pattern in India, with early-onset diabetes.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest benign liver tumour, and the imaging feature that identifies it, are
options: Focal nodular hyperplasia; a peripheral scar
Haemangioma; peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal filling on delayed phases
explanation: Biopsy is avoided for fear of bleeding. Focal nodular hyperplasia has a central, not peripheral, scar, and a hepatic adenoma in a woman on oral contraceptives carries bleeding and malignant risk.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A liver cyst with daughter cysts and a detached membrane on ultrasound is managed by
options: Albendazole cover with PAIR or surgery, avoiding spillage
explanation: Spillage of hydatid fluid risks anaphylaxis and secondary seeding, so scolicidal agents and careful isolation of the field are used. An amoebic abscess instead responds to metronidazole with aspiration only if large or left-lobed.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A patient has progressive dysphagia, first for solids then for liquids, with weight loss over 3 months. The first investigation is
explanation: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggests carcinoma, and endoscopy both visualises and samples the lesion. Endoscopic ultrasound then gives T and N staging, and CT or PET-CT detects distant disease.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Dysphagia that is worse for liquids than for solids and relieved by regurgitation suggests
explanation: Mechanical obstruction gives solid-predominant dysphagia, while a motility disorder affects liquids equally or more. Barium shows the bird-beak sign, and manometry is diagnostic.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Barrett oesophagus is defined by
options: Replacement of squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells
explanation: It predisposes to adenocarcinoma of the lower third. Surveillance endoscopy intervals depend on dysplasia grade, and high-grade dysplasia is treated by endoscopic resection with radiofrequency ablation.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus differs from adenocarcinoma in that it
options: Affects the lower third and arises in Barrett metaplasia
Affects the upper and middle thirds and is linked to smoking, alcohol, achalasia and corrosive stricture
Is commoner in obesity with reflux
explanation: Plummer–Vinson syndrome, tylosis and hot beverages are further risks. Adenocarcinoma is lower-third, reflux and obesity related, and is now commoner in Western countries.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest site of a pharyngeal pouch and its mechanism are
options: The piriform fossa, from tumour infiltration
Killian dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus, from failure of cricopharyngeal relaxation
The mid-oesophagus, from traction by nodes
explanation: It is a pulsion, false diverticulum of mucosa only. Endoscopic stapled diverticulotomy is the usual treatment. Option D describes a traction diverticulum from mediastinal tuberculosis.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Boerhaave syndrome is
options: A mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction causing haematemesis
Full-thickness spontaneous oesophageal rupture after forceful vomiting, usually in the left lower posterolateral wall
explanation: Option B is a Mallory–Weiss tear, which is mucosal and usually self-limiting. Boerhaave syndrome gives Mackler triad of vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema, and needs urgent repair or drainage.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A child who swallowed a strong alkali 3 weeks ago now has dysphagia. The likely finding and its management are
options: A corrosive stricture, managed by endoscopic dilatation
explanation: Alkalis cause deep liquefactive necrosis, so strictures are commoner than after acid ingestion. Neither emesis nor neutralisation is induced acutely, and the long-term risk of squamous carcinoma persists for decades.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In the Nissen fundoplication for gastro-oesophageal reflux, the wrap is
options: A 360-degree posterior wrap of the fundus around the lower oesophagus
explanation: Option C describes the Toupet partial fundoplication, which is chosen when oesophageal motility is impaired, because a complete wrap would then cause dysphagia. Gas-bloat syndrome follows an overtight wrap.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A patient with a chronic duodenal ulcer develops non-bilious vomiting of undigested food with a succussion splash. The complication is
explanation: Scarring at the pylorus is the cause, producing a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Correction of the electrolytes precedes endoscopic dilatation or surgery.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The biochemical disturbance of prolonged gastric outlet obstruction is
options: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
explanation: When sodium must be conserved, the distal tubule exchanges it for hydrogen rather than the depleted potassium, so the urine turns acid despite systemic alkalosis. Saline with potassium corrects it.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Free gas under the diaphragm with sudden severe epigastric pain and board-like rigidity indicates
options: A perforated peptic ulcer requiring resuscitation and operative repair with an omental patch
explanation: An erect chest film shows free gas in about 75% of cases, so its absence does not exclude perforation and CT is more sensitive. *Helicobacter pylori* eradication follows repair.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which is the commonest site of gastric carcinoma, and which lesion is a recognised premalignant condition?
options: Antrum and pylorus; chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia
explanation: Pernicious anaemia, partial gastrectomy, adenomatous polyps and *Helicobacter pylori* infection also predispose. A duodenal ulcer, in contrast, is not premalignant.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which eponymous sign of metastatic gastric carcinoma is a palpable left supraclavicular node?
explanation: The thoracic duct drains there. A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is umbilical, Blumer shelf is a rectal-shelf deposit in the pouch of Douglas, and a Krukenberg tumour is an ovarian metastasis with signet-ring cells.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A submucosal gastric tumour positive for CD117 (c-KIT) on immunohistochemistry is treated with
options: Radical gastrectomy with D2 nodal clearance in all cases
Surgical resection, with imatinib for high-risk or unresectable disease
explanation: A gastrointestinal stromal tumour arises from the interstitial cells of Cajal and spreads haematogenously, so wide nodal dissection is unnecessary. Size and mitotic index determine risk.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Early dumping syndrome after gastric surgery is caused by
options: Rapid entry of a hyperosmolar load into the jejunum with fluid shift
explanation: It occurs within 30 minutes with abdominal and vasomotor symptoms. Option B is late dumping, 2 to 3 hours after a meal. Both are managed with small, dry, low-carbohydrate meals, and octreotide if refractory.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The bariatric procedure that works chiefly by restriction without any intestinal bypass is
explanation: It also reduces ghrelin by removing the fundus. Surgery is considered at a BMI of 40, or 35 with comorbidity, with lower thresholds used in Asian populations. Bypass procedures add malabsorption and need lifelong supplements.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of small bowel obstruction in a patient with a previous laparotomy is
explanation: Hernia leads in the unoperated abdomen. Non-operative management with decompression and fluids succeeds in most adhesive obstructions, but strangulation — constant pain, tenderness, fever, acidosis — demands surgery.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Erect abdominal radiography showing multiple central air-fluid levels with a stepladder pattern indicates obstruction of the
explanation: Valvulae conniventes cross the whole lumen and the loops lie centrally. Large bowel obstruction shows peripheral distension with haustral markings that do not cross completely, and a caecal diameter above 12 cm risks perforation.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A coffee-bean sign on abdominal radiography in an elderly constipated patient suggests
explanation: A long mesentery with a narrow base allows twisting. Flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression with a flatus tube succeeds in most, and elective sigmoid resection follows because recurrence is common.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 9-month-old has colicky pain, vomiting, redcurrant-jelly stools and a sausage-shaped mass. The treatment of choice is
options: Pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction under imaging guidance
explanation: Ultrasound shows target and pseudokidney signs. Ileocolic intussusception in this age group usually follows lymphoid hyperplasia. Surgery is needed for peritonitis, failed reduction or a pathological lead point.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which feature favours appendicitis over mesenteric adenitis in a child?
options: Generalised shifting tenderness with cervical lymphadenopathy
Pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa with localised guarding
explanation: Visceral pain is referred to the umbilicus until the parietal peritoneum is involved. Fever before pain, and a preceding upper respiratory infection, favour mesenteric adenitis. Scoring systems such as Alvarado aid decisions.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A patient presents on day 6 of right iliac fossa pain with a tender mass and no peritonitis. The accepted management is
options: Ochsner–Sherren conservative regimen with antibiotics, and interval appendicectomy if indicated
explanation: Operating through an inflamed mass risks injury to adherent bowel. Failure to settle, or an abscess, prompts drainage. A mass in an older patient needs colonoscopy to exclude carcinoma.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest tumour of the appendix is
options: A neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour, usually at the tip
explanation: Appendicectomy suffices for a tumour below 1 cm, while one above 2 cm, or at the base with mesoappendiceal invasion, needs right hemicolectomy. Rupture of a mucinous tumour causes pseudomyxoma peritonei.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which colonic condition is characterised by crypt abscesses, continuous mucosal involvement from the rectum and pseudopolyps?
explanation: Toxic megacolon, perforation and colorectal carcinoma are the serious complications, and surveillance colonoscopy begins about 8 years after onset of pancolitis. Proctocolectomy with an ileal pouch is curative.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Screening colonoscopy for average-risk individuals conventionally begins at
explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis is screened from about 10 to 12 years, and Lynch syndrome from 20 to 25 years or 10 years before the youngest family case. A faecal immunochemical test is the alternative screen.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from a germline mutation in
explanation: Carcinoma is inevitable without prophylactic proctocolectomy. Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome with microsatellite instability, and *STK11* causes Peutz–Jeghers syndrome with hamartomatous polyps.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In carcinoma of the rectum 4 cm from the anal verge, the operation usually required is
options: Abdominoperineal resection with a permanent colostomy
explanation: A distal margin cannot be achieved without sacrificing the sphincter at this level. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy may downstage the tumour, and total mesorectal excision is the key oncological principle.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding in an elderly patient is
explanation: Angiodysplasia is next. Colonoscopy after bowel preparation locates and treats most, and CT angiography is used when bleeding is brisk. An upper source must always be excluded first.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Second-degree haemorrhoids are those that
options: Prolapse on straining and reduce spontaneously
explanation: First degree bleed only, third degree need manual reduction and fourth degree stay prolapsed. First and second degree respond to diet and banding, while third and fourth usually need haemorrhoidectomy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest site of an anal fissure and the key element of its treatment are
options: The posterior midline; relief of internal sphincter spasm with topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem
explanation: The posterior midline is relatively ischaemic. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the surgical standard for chronic fissure; multiple or lateral fissures suggest Crohn disease, tuberculosis or HIV.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Goodsall rule predicts that
options: A posterior external opening tracks curvilinearly to the posterior midline, while an anterior one tracks radially
Anterior openings track to the posterior midline
explanation: Low fistulae are treated by fistulotomy, while a high or complex track needs a seton, advancement flap or LIFT procedure to protect continence. MRI maps complex disease.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An inguinal hernia whose neck lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is
explanation: It pushes through the weak posterior wall at Hesselbach triangle and rarely reaches the scrotum. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the vessels and is the commoner type at all ages.
exam: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (direct versus indirect inguinal hernia, 2X)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET / 2018 NEET-PG (direct versus indirect inguinal hernia, 2X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Hesselbach triangle is bounded by
options: The deep ring, the superficial ring and the pubic tubercle
The inguinal ligament, the femoral vein and the pectineal line
The conjoint tendon, the lacunar ligament and the femoral artery
The inferior epigastric vessels, the inguinal ligament and the lateral border of rectus abdominis
explanation: A direct hernia emerges through it. Option B approximates the femoral canal's boundaries, where a femoral hernia descends below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A femoral hernia requires early repair chiefly because
options: Its narrow, rigid neck gives a high risk of strangulation
explanation: The lacunar ligament makes the neck unyielding. It is commoner in women, lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and is repaired by the low Lockwood, high McEvedy or inguinal Lotheissen approach.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In a Richter hernia
options: A Meckel diverticulum is the content
Two loops of bowel are contained with an intervening loop in the abdomen
Part of the circumference of the bowel wall is strangulated without complete obstruction
explanation: Diagnosis is easily delayed because obstruction is absent. Option B is a Maydl hernia, option C a Littre hernia and option D an Amyand hernia.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The Lichtenstein repair of an inguinal hernia is
options: Darning with the conjoint tendon sutured to the inguinal ligament
Approximation of the transversalis fascia to the iliopubic tract
Tension-free mesh reinforcement of the posterior wall
explanation: Tension-free repair reduced recurrence sharply over tissue repairs. Option D, herniotomy alone, is appropriate in children, where the defect is a patent processus vaginalis rather than a weak wall.

subject: General Surgery
stem: During thyroidectomy, which nerve lies closest to the inferior thyroid artery and risks injury causing hoarseness?
options: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
explanation: It supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery, and its injury causes loss of high-pitched phonation.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after thyroidectomy presents with
options: Complete loss of voice with a safe airway
Stridor and airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention
explanation: Both cords lie near the midline in a paramedian position, narrowing the glottis. Unilateral injury gives a hoarse, breathy voice that often improves as the opposite cord compensates.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia presenting on the second day is
options: Transient parathyroid ischaemia or inadvertent removal
explanation: Perioral tingling with Chvostek and Trousseau signs appears, and intravenous calcium gluconate is given for severe symptoms. Hungry bone syndrome follows parathyroidectomy for long-standing hyperparathyroidism, not thyroidectomy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The investigation of choice for a solitary thyroid nodule is
options: Fine-needle aspiration cytology with ultrasound characterisation
explanation: TSH is measured first, and a radioiodine scan is only useful when TSH is suppressed, suggesting a toxic nodule. The Bethesda system classifies cytology and guides whether surgery is needed.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which thyroid malignancy cannot be diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration cytology, and why?
options: Medullary carcinoma, because calcitonin cannot be stained
Papillary carcinoma, because of its nuclear features
Follicular carcinoma, because capsular or vascular invasion must be seen histologically
explanation: Cytology cannot separate a follicular adenoma from a carcinoma, so lobectomy is performed for histology. Papillary carcinoma shows Orphan Annie nuclei and psammoma bodies on cytology.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid differs from follicular carcinoma in that it
options: Spreads by blood to bone and lung
Spreads mainly by lymphatics and is multifocal, with an excellent prognosis
explanation: Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone and lung. Both are of follicular cell origin, take up radioiodine and are followed with thyroglobulin after total thyroidectomy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is monitored with which marker, and arises from which cell?
explanation: It shows amyloid stroma on histology, does not take up radioiodine and needs total thyroidectomy with central nodal clearance. A *RET* mutation must be sought, and phaeochromocytoma excluded before surgery.

subject: General Surgery
stem: MEN 2A consists of
options: Medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia
Medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and mucosal neuromas with a marfanoid habitus
explanation: Option C is MEN 2B, which lacks parathyroid disease but adds mucosal neuromas and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Option B is MEN 1, caused by a *MEN1* menin mutation rather than *RET*.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In a patient with phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma, the correct operative sequence is
options: Adrenalectomy first, after adequate alpha blockade
explanation: An unprepared phaeochromocytoma can cause a fatal hypertensive crisis during any operation. Phenoxybenzamine is given for 10 to 14 days with liberal salt and fluid, and a beta blocker added only afterwards.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is
explanation: It accounts for about 85% of cases. Sestamibi scanning with ultrasound localises it, and focused parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring is the operation. Hyperplasia is typical of MEN 1 and renal disease.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease that persists after a successful renal transplant is termed
explanation: The chronically stimulated glands become autonomous, giving hypercalcaemia with a high PTH where secondary disease had shown low or normal calcium. Subtotal parathyroidectomy is usually needed.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An incidentally discovered adrenal mass should be evaluated for
options: Hormonal activity and malignant risk, with size, imaging phenotype and metanephrines all assessed
explanation: Biopsy is avoided until phaeochromocytoma is excluded, because it can provoke a crisis. Resection is advised for a functioning lesion, a mass above about 4 cm, or suspicious imaging features.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Conn syndrome is treated by
options: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy for a unilateral adenoma, and spironolactone for bilateral hyperplasia
explanation: Adrenal vein sampling separates the two when imaging is equivocal. Hypertension with hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, and a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio, are the clue.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood arising from the adrenal medulla is
explanation: It crosses the midline and displaces the kidney, whereas a Wilms tumour arises within the kidney and distorts the calyces. Raised urinary vanillylmandelic and homovanillic acid, and *MYCN* amplification, characterise it.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest composition of renal stones overall is
explanation: Struvite stones follow urease-producing infection and form staghorn calculi, uric acid stones are radiolucent and dissolve with urinary alkalinisation, and cystine stones are faintly radio-opaque and recur in young patients.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A radiolucent renal stone on plain radiography that is visible on non-contrast CT is most likely
explanation: Only pure matrix stones and indinavir stones are missed by CT. Uric acid stones are managed with hydration, allopurinol and potassium citrate to raise urinary pH above 6.5, and often dissolve without intervention.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Cystine stones are characteristic of
options: Cystinuria, a defect of dibasic amino acid transport in the proximal tubule
explanation: Cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine are all poorly reabsorbed, but only cystine is insoluble. Hexagonal crystals appear in urine; treatment is high fluid intake, alkalinisation and penicillamine or tiopronin.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 7 mm stone in the lower ureter with no obstruction or infection in a well patient is best managed by
options: Medical expulsive therapy with analgesia and hydration, with ureteroscopy if it fails
explanation: Stones below 10 mm often pass spontaneously. Fever, obstruction of a single kidney, or uncontrolled pain demand urgent drainage by a DJ stent or percutaneous nephrostomy before any definitive procedure.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (renal stone management and DJ stenting, 2X)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (renal stone management and DJ stenting, 2X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: The indication for emergency decompression with a DJ stent or nephrostomy in ureteric colic is
options: Obstruction with fever or deteriorating renal function
explanation: An infected, obstructed system is a urological emergency that can progress to septic shock within hours. Definitive stone treatment is deferred until the infection is controlled.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Sterile pyuria with frequency and a putty kidney on imaging suggests
explanation: Early morning urine for acid-fast bacilli or nucleic acid testing is diagnostic. A golf-hole ureteric orifice, thimble bladder and ureteric strictures are the other classic features; treatment is medical with surgery for strictures.
exam: 2022 INI-CET (genitourinary tuberculosis — sterile pyuria, putty kidney, golf-hole ureter, 3X)

metadata.basedOn: 2022 INI-CET (genitourinary tuberculosis — sterile pyuria, putty kidney, golf-hole ureter, 3X)

subject: General Surgery
stem: Painless gross haematuria in a 60-year-old smoker should first be investigated by
explanation: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder must be excluded; smoking, aniline dyes and cyclophosphamide are the risk factors. Ultrasound alone misses small tumours and upper tract lesions.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Non-muscle-invasive bladder carcinoma that is high grade is treated with
options: Transurethral resection followed by intravesical BCG
explanation: BCG provokes a local immune response that lowers recurrence and progression. Muscle-invasive disease needs radical cystectomy with urinary diversion, preceded by neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A patient with an ileal conduit develops a metabolic disturbance. The expected pattern is
explanation: Intestinal mucosa absorbs chloride and ammonium from urine while secreting bicarbonate. The disturbance is worse with longer segments and with colonic rather than ileal use, and is treated with oral bicarbonate.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A male neonate has a distended bladder, poor urinary stream and bilateral hydronephrosis. The diagnosis and first step are
options: Posterior urethral valves; bladder drainage with a catheter, then a micturating cystourethrogram
Neurogenic bladder; clean intermittent catheterisation only
explanation: A keyhole sign appears on antenatal ultrasound. Decompression protects the kidneys, and definitive treatment is endoscopic valve ablation. It is the commonest cause of bladder outlet obstruction in a male infant.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest zone of origin of prostatic carcinoma, and of benign hyperplasia, are respectively
explanation: This is why carcinoma is palpable on rectal examination while hyperplasia causes outflow symptoms. Systematic biopsy therefore samples the peripheral zone, now usually guided by multiparametric MRI.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Metastatic prostate carcinoma is initially treated by
options: Androgen deprivation with a GnRH agonist plus initial anti-androgen cover, or orchidectomy
explanation: A GnRH agonist causes an initial testosterone flare that can worsen bone pain or cord compression, which the anti-androgen prevents. Osteoblastic bone deposits via the vertebral venous plexus are characteristic.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A 25-year-old has a painless, firm testicular swelling that does not transilluminate, with a raised AFP and beta-hCG. The first step is
options: Inguinal orchidectomy with high cord ligation after tumour markers and imaging
explanation: A scrotal approach risks seeding to the inguinal nodes and altering the lymphatic drainage, which is normally to the para-aortic nodes. A raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Sudden severe testicular pain with a high-riding transverse testis and absent cremasteric reflex in a 14-year-old requires
options: Immediate scrotal exploration with bilateral fixation
explanation: Salvage falls steeply after about 6 hours, so imaging must not delay surgery. The contralateral testis is fixed because the bell-clapper deformity is usually bilateral.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An undescended testis should be brought down by orchidopexy preferably by
explanation: Early surgery limits germ cell loss and makes later examination possible, though the raised malignancy risk is not abolished. An impalpable testis is assessed by laparoscopy, the investigation of choice.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A scrotal swelling that transilluminates and in which the testis cannot be felt separately is
explanation: Ultrasound is needed in a young adult to exclude an underlying tumour causing a secondary hydrocele. A varicocele feels like a bag of worms, does not transilluminate, and on the left may signal a renal tumour.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The six Ps of acute limb ischaemia include all EXCEPT
explanation: The six are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and perishing cold. Paraesthesia and paralysis mark a threatened limb that needs revascularisation within hours, before fixed mottling appears.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation has sudden onset of a cold, pulseless, painful leg with preserved sensation. The management is
explanation: Sudden onset in a patient with a cardiac source suggests embolism rather than thrombosis in situ. The common femoral bifurcation is the commonest lodging site; reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome must be anticipated.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The most dangerous metabolic consequence of reperfusion after prolonged limb ischaemia is
options: Hyperkalaemia with myoglobinuric renal failure and acidosis
explanation: Potassium, myoglobin and acid metabolites wash out of necrotic muscle. Aggressive fluids, urine alkalinisation, potassium management and fasciotomy are needed, and primary amputation is chosen for an unsalvageable limb.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An ankle-brachial pressure index of 0.45 in a claudicant indicates
options: Medial calcification giving a falsely low value
explanation: Normal is 0.9 to 1.3; 0.4 to 0.9 is claudication and below 0.4 indicates critical ischaemia. Diabetic medial calcification produces a falsely **high** index, so toe pressures or waveforms are used instead.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Buttock and thigh claudication with impotence and absent femoral pulses is
explanation: Superficial femoral disease instead gives calf claudication with a present femoral pulse, the commonest pattern. Aortobifemoral bypass or endovascular reconstruction is the treatment.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) differs from atherosclerosis in that it
options: Affects small and medium distal vessels in young male smokers, with migratory thrombophlebitis
Affects large proximal vessels in the elderly
explanation: Complete tobacco cessation is the only intervention that alters its course, as distal disease leaves no suitable bypass target. A corkscrew collateral pattern appears on angiography.

subject: General Surgery
stem: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is generally offered elective repair at a diameter of
options: 5.5 cm, or when expanding faster than 1 cm per year, or when symptomatic
explanation: Below that, rupture risk is lower than operative risk. Rupture classically gives pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass; a stable patient is imaged by CT, while an unstable one goes straight to theatre.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Trendelenburg test in varicose veins assesses
options: Saphenofemoral junction and deep-to-superficial valvular competence
explanation: Duplex ultrasound has largely replaced it and maps reflux precisely. Perthes test assesses deep venous patency, which must be confirmed before any superficial vein is stripped or ablated.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A venous ulcer differs from an arterial ulcer in that it is typically
options: At the medial malleolus, shallow with sloping edges, in a limb with oedema and pigmentation
On the toes and heel, deep with punched-out edges
On the sole, painless with callus
Over the sacrum with undermined edges
explanation: Graduated compression after excluding arterial disease by ABPI is the mainstay. Option C describes a neuropathic diabetic ulcer and option D a pressure sore.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Lymphoedema differs from venous oedema chiefly in that it
options: Is non-pitting with a positive Stemmer sign and skin thickening
explanation: Filariasis is the commonest cause worldwide and axillary dissection the commonest iatrogenic one. Treatment is decongestive physiotherapy with compression; recurrent cellulitis is the main complication.

subject: General Surgery
stem: Which suture material is absorbable and monofilament, suited to bowel anastomosis?
explanation: Monofilament sutures harbour fewer bacteria than braided ones, and PDS retains strength for about 6 weeks. Silk is braided and non-absorbable, while polypropylene is non-absorbable and used for vascular and mesh work.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A Doyen retractor and a Babcock forceps are used respectively for
options: Retracting the abdominal wall, and holding bowel or tubular structures atraumatically
Holding drapes, and retracting the liver
explanation: Instrument recognition is asked almost every paper. A crushing clamp such as Payr is used on the specimen side, while an occlusion clamp such as Doyen's intestinal clamp protects the retained bowel.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The chief advantage of a closed suction (Redivac) drain over a corrugated open drain is
options: A lower risk of ascending infection with measurable output
explanation: Open drains leave a route for skin organisms to track inwards. A suction drain is avoided next to a fresh bowel anastomosis, where negative pressure could promote a fistula.

subject: General Surgery
stem: The commonest cause of fever on the first postoperative day is
options: Atelectasis, from hypoventilation and retained secretions
explanation: The classic timeline runs wind, water, wound, walking and wonder drugs — atelectasis on day 1 to 2, urinary infection on day 3 to 5, wound infection on day 5 to 7, and thrombosis after day 5.

subject: General Surgery
stem: In live-related renal transplantation, the single most important immunological requirement is
options: ABO compatibility with a negative crossmatch
explanation: A positive crossmatch means preformed donor-specific antibodies and predicts hyperacute rejection. HLA matching improves graft survival but is not absolutely required, and the graft is placed extraperitoneally in the iliac fossa.

subject: General Surgery
stem: A hypertrophic scar differs from a keloid in that it
options: Stays within the original wound margins and tends to regress with time
Extends beyond the wound margins and recurs after excision
explanation: Option B describes a keloid, which is commoner over the sternum, shoulder and earlobe and in darker skin. Both respond to intralesional triamcinolone, pressure and silicone, and keloid excision needs adjuvant treatment.
